clinicalPearls: A halophilic, curved Gram-negative bacillus found in warm coastal and estuarine seawater, especially during warmer months
Two classic presentations: fulminant primary septicaemia after eating raw or undercooked shellfish (particularly oysters), and rapidly progressive wound infection after seawater or shellfish exposure
Hosts with chronic liver disease, haemochromatosis or other iron-overload states, and immunosuppression are at greatly increased risk of overwhelming disease
Characteristic haemorrhagic bullae and rapidly spreading cellulitis progressing to necrotising fasciitis are hallmark cutaneous findings
Empirical therapy pairs a tetracycline such as doxycycline with a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftazidime, alongside aggressive resuscitation
Early and repeated surgical debridement or fasciotomy is essential when soft-tissue necrosis is present
Mortality is high in septicaemic disease, so treatment must not await culture confirmation when the exposure history and clinical picture fit
reference.pathophysiology: Vibrio vulnificus is a salt-requiring marine bacterium that causes disease when ingested in contaminated shellfish or when it enters through a break in the skin exposed to seawater. It expresses a polysaccharide capsule that resists phagocytosis and complement, together with cytolysins, proteases and other exotoxins that damage tissue and increase vascular permeability. Free iron promotes rapid bacterial growth, which is why individuals with cirrhosis or iron-overload states are so susceptible to fulminant bloodstream invasion. The resulting endotoxaemia and toxin release produce septic shock, and local toxin activity generates the characteristic haemorrhagic bullae and necrotising soft-tissue destruction.
additionalDifferentials: Other marine Vibrio species infections including Vibrio alginolyticus
additionalInvestigations: Blood cultures, which frequently yield the organism in septicaemic disease
Culture of aspirate or tissue from bullae and wounds, ideally on selective media such as TCBS agar
Gram stain of blister fluid or wound exudate showing curved Gram-negative bacilli
Assessment of liver function and ferritin/iron studies to identify predisposing states
Full blood count, lactate, renal function and coagulation profile to gauge severity of sepsis
Cross-sectional imaging of the affected limb to define the extent of deep soft-tissue involvement
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging haemorrhagic bullae with severe pain out of proportion to skin findings
Hypotension and signs of septic shock following recent shellfish ingestion or seawater exposure
Known cirrhosis or iron-overload state in a patient with a marine exposure and systemic illness
Clinical or imaging evidence of necrotising fasciitis requiring emergency surgery
reference.prognosis: Wound infections treated early with appropriate antibiotics and debridement often recover, but primary septicaemia carries very high mortality, particularly in those with liver disease, and outcome depends heavily on rapid antibiotic and surgical intervention.
pitfalls: Attributing early leg pain and fever to simple cellulitis and delaying surgical assessment
Failing to elicit the marine or shellfish exposure history in a septic patient
Overlooking underlying cirrhosis or haemochromatosis that dramatically raises risk
Delaying combination antibiotics while awaiting microbiological confirmation
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Prompt empirical antibiotics combining a tetracycline such as doxycycline with a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftazidime, a fluoroquinolone being an alternative
Early and repeated surgical debridement or fasciotomy when soft-tissue necrosis or necrotising fasciitis is present
Aggressive fluid resuscitation and sepsis management, with vasopressor and organ support for septic shock
Intensive care support with monitoring of lactate, renal function and coagulation to gauge and manage sepsis severity
Counsel high-risk hosts with chronic liver disease or iron-overload states to avoid raw shellfish and seawater exposure of wounds
Involve infectious diseases, surgery and critical care early given the fulminant course and high mortality
